title: Host Discovery
body: Turning IPs into an attack map. Two rules: (1) match the method to your VANTAGE - ARP/ICMP work on a LOCAL subnet but are useless THROUGH A PIVOT (L2 dies at the tunnel, ICMP gets filtered), so pivoted discovery is TCP-only. (2) Don't stop at live IPs - RESOLVE NAMES. Reverse-resolving SMB hosts to FQDN exposes the domain, the hostnames (FILES02, DEV04), and - critically - the DC. An IP list is lame; a named domain map with the DC identified is the actual goal.
cmd:
# ========== PICK YOUR CONTEXT ==========
# On the LOCAL subnet (direct L2 access): ARP works, use it - unblockable.
# THROUGH A PIVOT (ligolo/proxychains): ARP + ICMP are USELESS (L2 dies at the
#   tunnel, ICMP gets filtered). Discover hosts by TCP instead. See pivot_portscan.

# ========== LOCAL SUBNET (direct) ==========
sudo arp-scan -I $iface $subnet | tee arp.txt        # most reliable on-subnet
sudo nmap -sn $subnet -oG ping.txt                   # ICMP/ARP combo
fping -a -g $subnet 2>/dev/null | tee fping.txt
cat arp.txt fping.txt | grep -oE '([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}' | sort -u > live_hosts.txt

# ========== THROUGH A PIVOT (TCP discovery) ==========
# ICMP lies over ligolo (Destination Host Unreachable even when host is UP).
# A host is "live" if ANY common port answers. --open cuts the phantoms.
nmap -sT -Pn -p 445,135,139,3389,5985,80,22,88,389 $subnet --open -oG tcp_disc.txt
grep -oE '([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}' tcp_disc.txt | sort -u > live_hosts.txt
#  >> if a sweep says ALL 255 hosts are 'up' = false positive (ICMP/gateway
#     answering for the range). Trust --open TCP results, not ping counts. <<

# ========== RESOLVE NAMES = EXPOSE THE DOMAIN ==========
# This is the step that turns IPs into an attack map. nxc reverse-resolves
# SMB hosts to FQDN + domain in one shot:
nxc smb $subnet                      # name:HOST  domain:CORP.COM  (signing/SMBv1)
nxc smb $subnet --generate-hosts-file hosts.txt    # ready-made /etc/hosts block
#   -> tells you hostnames (FILES02, DEV04...), the DOMAIN, and OS in one pass.

# Seed /etc/hosts so kerberos/ldap tooling resolves names (BACK IT UP FIRST):
sudo cp /etc/hosts /etc/hosts.bak.$(date +%F_%H%M%S)
# then append the  IP  FQDN  HOST  lines (nxc --generate-hosts-file gives these)

# ========== FIND THE DC (do NOT skip) ==========
# The box answering Kerberos(88) + LDAP(389) + GC(3268) is the domain controller.
nmap -sT -Pn -p 88,389,3268,445,53 $subnet --open
nxc smb $subnet | grep -i "domain controller"        # nxc flags DCs
nslookup -type=SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.<DOMAIN> <any_internal_dns_ip>
#  DC missing from THIS subnet? it's behind another hop - the domain-joined
#  members can reach it even if your pivot host can't. (see double_pivot)

# ========== VALIDATED: MEDTECH (PG-style DMZ->internal) ==========
# Landed SYSTEM on WEB02 (DMZ, non-domain-joined, dmz.corp). ligolo up to the
# internal 172.16.x. TCP sweep + nxc resolved the whole domain:
#   .11 FILES02  .12 DEV04  .13 PROD01  .82/.83 CLIENTxx  .254 WEB02(pivot NIC)
# WEB02's nltest gave NO_SUCH_DOMAIN (it's DMZ) - the DC sits with the members,
# reachable only once the pivot's up. A domain user (joe) was useless on WEB02
# but became the key to enumerating every internal box. Names first, then joe.
warn: Through a pivot, ICMP/ping LIES - a sweep reporting all 255 hosts 'up' is a false positive (gateway answering for the range); trust --open TCP results only. Always back up /etc/hosts before seeding names. And always scan 88/389/3268 to find the DC - if it's not on this subnet it's behind another hop, not absent.
